newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Britain's David Hannay in Cyprus ahead of UN talks.
newsitem.headline: Britain's David Hannay in Cyprus ahead of UN talks.

text.p: Britain's special envoy on the Cyprus question said on Sunday there was more common ground between the two sides on the divided island than either cared to admit.
Sir David Hannay said neither side in the conflict was willing to make commitments on one subject before the other side committed itself on another issue.

Cyprus President Glafcos Clerides, as Greek Cypriot leader, and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash are expected to hold U.N.-sponsored talks on July 9 in New York, their first in three years, to try to end the 23-year division of Cyprus.
Last week U.S. President Bill Clinton appointed Richard Holbrooke, negotiator of the 1995 Bosnia peace accord, as special emissary for Cyprus.
"I do not agree that there has not been the identification of any common ground," said Hannay, in Cyprus to assist United Nations preparations for the direct talks. "It has not been registered."

The British diplomat, on his sixth visit to the eastern Mediterranean island since he assumed duties as Britain's special envoy last year, will have separate meetings with the leaders on both sides of the divide before leaving on Wednesday.
One of his tasks will be to identify the most significant areas of disagreement.

"If I stood here and identified the aspects, and indeed any aspects, tomorrow morning several people would immediately deny this was common ground or had been agreed so I shall not do so," Hannay replied when asked where common ground has been found.
The Greek Cypriot-led government has said that the proximity talks have failed to bridge the gap between the two sides.

Hannay cautioned against being too pessimistic or optimistic on the outcome of the talks next month. "I think somewhere between the extremes of pessimism and optimism, with a lot of realism, is the right place to be," he said.

Mainland Turkish troops invaded Cyprus in 1974 following a short-lived Greek Cypriot coup in Nicosia engineered by the military then ruling Greece. Some 30,000 troops remain in a Turkish-Cypriot mini-state that only Ankara recognises in the northern part of the island.

International mediation attempts to reunite Cyprus as a bi-zonal bicommunal federal state have recently gained pace as the Cyprus government prepares for membership talks with the European Union next year, and amid increased concern at the risks of growing militarisation of the island.

Hannay said the purpose of the negotiations next month was to go beyond the generalities of the already agreed principles of the final solution, that of a federal state, and tackle specific issues. He mentioned the issue of rotating presidency -- rejected by the Greek Cypriots -- and powers of co-decision in a federal government as an example.

The conflict is a source of contention between NATO partners Greece and Turkey, generally regarded as the respective motherlands of the two communities. Turkey and Greece, with Britain, are guarantors of Cyprus under the 1960 constitution. Athens also has a defence pact with the Greek Cypriots.
